People exchange their views in a conversation.
Pexels · 9811867
Making disagreement productive
Collaboration gains value from constructive disagreement, not merely smooth agreement. Two conditions make dissent productive: a shared
purpose that disciplines the discussion and relevant evidence that helps participants revise their views.
A shared purpose gives disagreement a useful boundary. In a community exhibition project, debates about the format initially reflected
personal preferences. Once the team agreed that residents’ access mattered most, we could distinguish essential requirements from choices
open to negotiation.
Evidence then turns that common purpose into better decisions. Residents’ feedback revealed that the proposed layout was difficult to
navigate. This concrete finding allowed us to reconcile accessibility with creative ambitions, replacing competing tastes with a problem we
could solve together.
Constructive disagreement thus depends on both common aims and a willingness to respond to evidence. Consensus is more valuable when
it emerges from this inquiry. Good collaboration makes the reasoning behind agreement visible rather than treating agreement itself as proof of
success.
BUILD YOUR OWN · State a clear main idea; develop two different points with examples; bring them together in the conclusion. Each body
paragraph needs a distinct point and a concrete example. The conclusion should connect the argument rather than introduce a new proposal.
Persuade a group to change how they listen to a friend. Support your recommendation with two different reasons and a practical example of
each. Use four short paragraphs: introduction, two developed points, and conclusion. (Model: One possible outline: introduce the situation;
discuss asking an open question gives the other person room to explain with an example; discuss checking our understanding prevents
unnecessary disagreement with a different example; conclude by connecting the two points.)
